title: Tracking, advanced
summary: How serious operators connect every click to the deposit it produced: trackers, click IDs, server-side events, the conversions API, deduplication and postback mapping. Clean, consented data is what lets the ad platform find more people who actually deposit.

lessons.title: Trackers and click IDs
objectives: By the end you can explain what an ad tracker does and when you need one
By the end you can follow a click ID from ad to postback
By the end you can set up sub IDs so every conversion carries its campaign, ad set and ad
By the end you can choose between redirect and direct tracking

steps.p: Advanced tracking rests on one idea. When someone clicks, you give that click a unique ID and carry it through every step: lander, offer, Telegram, deposit. When a conversion happens, the ID tells you exactly which ad paid for it. Without it, every kill or scale call is a guess with real money behind it.

d.b: Click ID in, click ID out
d.s: The thread that ties spend to revenue

steps.say: Advanced tracking rests on one simple idea. When someone clicks your ad, you give that click its own unique I D, and you carry it through every step: the lander, the offer, Telegram, the deposit. Look at the line on screen: click I D in, click I D out. When a conversion happens, that I D tells you exactly which ad paid for it. Without it, every kill or scale call is a guess, with real money behind it.

steps.p: A tracker is software that sits between your ads and your offers. It can be cloud-hosted or self-hosted on your own server. Its core jobs are the same everywhere.
steps.more: Common examples include Keitaro, Binom, RedTrack and Voluum. Named only as examples, not endorsements; features and prices change. A spreadsheet plus network reports works at small scale. Once you run several offers, geos or landers at once, a tracker saves you hours and shows profit in one place.
d: Counts clicks|with a unique ID each
Routes traffic|to landers and offers you choose
Reports|profit by campaign, ad, geo, device
steps.say: So what is a tracker? It's software that sits between your ads and your offers. It can live in the cloud, or on your own server. Look at the four cards. It counts clicks, giving each one a unique I D. It routes traffic to the landers and offers you choose. It receives postbacks, the conversions from the network. And it reports profit by campaign, ad, geo and device. Keitaro, Binom, RedTrack and Voluum are common examples, named only as examples, not endorsements. A spreadsheet works at small scale, but once you run several offers, geos or landers, a tracker saves you hours.

steps.h: The path of a click ID
steps.p: Example path for one trading-offer click. Each arrow is a handover where the ID can get lost, for example when a link is rebuilt by hand or a redirect drops parameters. Test every handover before launch.
steps.say: Follow this path from left to right. It's an example for one trading-offer click. The ad is clicked, the tracker makes an I D, the lander keeps it, the offer link carries it, the network stores it, and the postback returns it. Each arrow is a handover, and each handover is a place where the I D can get lost, for example when someone rebuilds a link by hand, or a redirect drops parameters. That's why you test every handover before launch.

steps.p: Each party in the chain creates its own ID. The ad platform has one, your tracker has one, the network stores yours, and Telegram has its own user ID. Your tracker's job is to link them together.
steps.say: Here's something that confuses beginners. Every party in the chain makes its own I D. Look down the table. Meta adds f b clid to the U R L after an ad click. TikTok adds t t clid. Your tracker makes its own click I D for every link you build. The network sub I D is something you fill, through sub one and so on. And Telegram has its own user I D in your bot's updates. Your tracker's job is to link all of these together.

steps.p: Most networks give you sub ID slots in the offer link. You fill them with tracker values so they come back in the postback. Slot names differ by network.
steps.say: Now, how does your click I D get into the network? Most networks give you sub I D slots in the offer link. Read the equation: the offer U R L, plus sub one equals click I D, plus sub two equals campaign, plus sub three equals ad. You fill these slots with tracker values, so they come back to you in the postback. One thing to watch: slot names differ by network, so check yours.

steps.h: Worked example: a tracked offer link
steps.p: Example: your tracker gives this click the ID 8f3k2a. The ad came from campaign NG_TRD_Broad, ad H2. The offer link carries all three, so a deposit next week comes back in the postback with the exact ad attached, and your report can credit H2.

d.text:
Template in your tracker:
https://track.network.example/click?offer=88&aff=5678&sub1={clickid}&sub2={campaign}&sub3={ad}

Filled at click time:
https://track.network.example/click?offer=88&aff=5678&sub1=8f3k2a&sub2=NG_TRD_Broad&sub3=H2
d.note: Example network and tracker. Macro names such as {clickid} vary by tracker; slot names such as sub1 vary by network.

steps.say: Here's a worked example. The code on screen shows a template in your tracker, and then the same link filled at click time. Say your tracker gives this click the I D eight f three k two a. The ad came from the campaign N G, T R D, Broad, ad H two. The offer link carries all three. So if that person deposits next week, the postback comes back with the exact ad attached, and your report credits H two. This is an example network and tracker, and macro and slot names vary.

steps.p: Redirect tracking sends the click through the tracker's domain before the page. Direct tracking loads your page first and records the visit with a script. Both are legitimate. Neither should ever show reviewers a different page from users.
steps.more: Meta and other platforms prefer that the ad's link and the final page share a clear, consistent domain and that everyone sees the same page. Using a tracker to show reviewers a safe page and users a different one is cloaking. It breaks every major platform's policy and leads to bans.

a.title: Redirect
items: Ad shows tracker domain unless set up well

b.title: Direct
items: Ad links straight to your page
Can miss visits if script blocked

steps.say: There are two ways to track. Look at the left side: redirect tracking sends the click through the tracker's domain before the page. It counts very reliably, but adds a small delay. On the right, direct tracking: the ad links straight to your page, and a script records the visit. It's faster and cleaner for ad review, but can miss visits if the script is blocked. Both are legitimate. But neither should ever show reviewers a different page from users. That's cloaking, it breaks every major platform's policy, and it leads to bans.

steps.p: Messy names make reports useless, because you cannot filter or group results. Agree a naming pattern with your whole team, write it down and use exactly the same pattern in ads, tracker and sheets.
d: Geo first: NG, KE, ZA, GH, CM
Same pattern in ads, tracker and sheet
steps.say: Messy names make reports useless, because you can't filter or group your results. So go down this checklist. Geo first: N G, K E, Z A, G H, C M. Then vertical and audience. No spaces, use underscores. Keep each value short. And use exactly the same pattern in your ads, your tracker and your sheet. Agree this pattern with your whole team and write it down, so everyone's reports mean the same thing.

steps.p: Example: 1,000 clicks where we checked how many still carried the click ID at each step. Losses usually come from links rebuilt by hand or redirects that drop parameters.
steps.say: This funnel shows where I Ds get lost. It's an example: one thousand ad clicks, and we checked how many still carried the click I D at each step. Nine hundred and sixty reached the lander with the I D. Three hundred and eighty offer clicks still had it. One hundred and twenty registrations carried sub one, and eighteen F T Ds, first time deposits, did. Losses usually come from links rebuilt by hand, or redirects that drop parameters.

steps.p: A tracker report puts spend, conversions and profit on one row per sub ID. Example, $40 payout: grouping by sub3, the ad, shows which ads paid for which deposits. The total looks fine, but two of the three ads lose money. Column names differ by tracker; check yours.
steps.more: Check: H1 6 × $40 = $240 − $262 = −$22. H2 14 × $40 = $560 − $372 = $188. H3 3 × $40 = $120 − $191 = −$71. Together: $825 spend, 23 FTDs, $920 revenue, $95 profit, all of it carried by H2. Without sub3 you would only see the total and keep paying for H1 and H3.
steps.say: Here's a tracker report, grouped by sub three, the ad. The payout is forty dollars, and this is example data. Look at the highlighted table. H one spent two hundred and sixty two dollars for six F T Ds, a loss of twenty two dollars. H two spent three hundred and seventy two for fourteen F T Ds, a profit of one hundred and eighty eight. H three lost seventy one. Together that's a ninety five dollar profit, all of it carried by H two. Without sub three, you'd only see the total, and keep paying for H one and H three.

steps.p: Before every launch, click your own ad preview, register on the offer as a test if the network allows it, and check that the conversion appears in your tracker with the right sub IDs. Ask your network manager how to run a test conversion.

d.text: One test conversion before launch saves days of untracked spend.

steps.say: Here's a habit that pays for itself. Before every launch, click your own ad preview. Register on the offer as a test, if the network allows it. Then check that the conversion appears in your tracker with the right sub I Ds. Your network manager can tell you how to run a test conversion. As the tip says, one test conversion before launch saves days of untracked spend.

steps.p: A key health number: the share of the network's conversions that your tracker can match to a click. Below this, your optimisation decisions are guesses.

d.label: of network conversions matched to a click
d.note: Example target. Rough guide, varies by setup.

steps.say: This is a key health number: the share of the network's conversions that your tracker can match to a click. Look at the figure on screen, ninety five percent. That's an example target, and a rough guide that varies by setup. The point is simple. If too many conversions can't be matched to a click, your optimisation decisions are guesses.

steps.p: Use the matched share as a gate. At 90% or more, trust ad-level numbers and apply the rule card from the Budget and kill rules module. Below 90%, stop making ad-level kill or scale calls and fix the lost IDs first. Starting rules; adapt them to your setup.

d.text: Example: network 50 FTDs, tracker matches 46: 92%, decide on ads. Tracker matches 35: 70%, fix tracking first.

steps.say: So use the matched share as a gate. At ninety percent or more, trust your ad-level numbers, and apply the rule card from the Budget and kill rules module. Below ninety percent, stop making ad-level kill or scale calls, and fix the lost I Ds first. Read the example: the network shows fifty F T Ds and your tracker matches forty six. That's ninety two percent, so you decide on ads. If it matches thirty five, that's seventy percent, so you fix tracking first. These are starting rules, adapt them to your setup.

steps.p: These mistakes cause most lost click IDs. None of them shows an error message. You only see them as a widening gap between what the network pays you for and what your tracker can trace to an ad.

a.title: Mistakes
items: Different names in ads and tracker

steps.say: These mistakes cause most lost click I Ds. Read the left column, then the fix beside it. Rebuilding links by hand: instead, copy links from the tracker. Different names in ads and tracker: use one naming pattern everywhere. A redirect that drops parameters: test every redirect hop. Optimising below ninety percent matched: fix matching before decisions. Never testing a conversion: do one test conversion per launch. None of these shows an error message. You only see a widening gap between what the network pays and what your tracker can trace.

steps.h: Trackers never hide pages from reviewers
steps.p: A tracker can route traffic, and that power is sometimes abused to show reviewers a safe page and users a different one. That is cloaking: it breaks every major platform's policy and gets accounts banned. Use routing only for real tests that everyone can see. More in the Ad account bans module.

d.text: If a tool sells "reviewer filtering" or "safe pages for moderators", it is a cloaking tool. Do not use it.

steps.say: One important warning. A tracker can route traffic, and that power is sometimes abused to show reviewers a safe page and users a different one. That's cloaking. It breaks every major platform's policy and gets accounts banned. Use routing only for real tests that everyone can see. And as the warning on screen says, if a tool sells reviewer filtering, or safe pages for moderators, it is a cloaking tool. Do not use it. There's more in the Ad account bans module.

takeaways: Give every click a unique ID and carry it through every step
Use the network's sub ID slots to send campaign, ad set and ad
Redirect and direct tracking both work; never show reviewers a different page
Test one conversion end to end before every launch

lessons.say_intro: In this lesson you'll learn what an ad tracker does and how one click I D can follow a person from your ad all the way to a deposit. This is the thread that ties your spend to your revenue, so every kill or scale call you make later depends on it.
lessons.say_outro: You've seen what a tracker does, how a click I D travels from ad to postback, how to fill sub I Ds, and why trackers never hide pages from reviewers. Your task: write your team's sub I D naming pattern on one line, then build one offer link with sub one, sub two and sub three filled, from your tracker or by hand. Now take the quiz.

lessons.title: Server-side events and the conversions API
objectives: By the end you can explain the difference between browser and server events
By the end you can list the fields that make a server event match a person
By the end you can send a server event for a Telegram join or deposit
By the end you can handle consent and hashing correctly

steps.p: A browser event is sent by the pixel script in the visitor's browser. A server event is sent by your server straight to the platform's API. Browser events are easy but can be blocked. Server events are reliable but need setup.

a.title: Browser (pixel)
items: Only sees what happens on the page

b.title: Server (CAPI)
items: Can send events after the visit
Can report Telegram joins and deposits

steps.say: Let's start with the two ways an event reaches the platform. On the left, a browser event, sent by the pixel script in the visitor's browser. It's easy, but some ad blockers and browser privacy rules can stop it, and it only sees what happens on the page. On the right, a server event, sent from your server straight to the platform's A P I, through C A P I, the Conversions A P I. It isn't affected by ad blockers, it can send events after the visit, and it can report Telegram joins and deposits. The trade-off is that it needs setup.

steps.p: Your most valuable events, a Telegram join, a registration at the broker, a first deposit, happen away from your page. A pixel never sees them. Only a server event can tell the ad platform that a specific ad click turned into a depositor.

d.b: The pixel cannot see a deposit
d.s: Your server can tell the platform

steps.say: Here's why this matters for you. Your most valuable events, a Telegram join, a registration at the broker, a first deposit, all happen away from your page. As the screen says, the pixel cannot see a deposit. Only a server event can tell the ad platform that a specific ad click turned into a depositor. And that's the signal you want the algorithm to learn from.

steps.h: How a server event reaches Meta
steps.p: Example flow for a deposit sent to Meta. The key is storing the fbclid with your own click ID at the moment of the click. Names change; check Meta's current Conversions API documentation before you build.
steps.say: Follow this flow for a deposit sent to Meta. It's an example. The ad click arrives with an f b clid. You store that f b clid together with your own click I D, right at the moment of the click. Later the network sends a postback for an F T D, a first time deposit. Your server builds the event, sends it to the Conversions A P I, and Meta matches it to a user. The key step is storing the f b clid at click time. Names change, so check Meta's current Conversions A P I documentation before you build.

steps.p: The platform needs enough information to know which person the event belongs to. More good fields mean better matching and better optimisation. Personal fields such as email and phone must be hashed before sending.
steps.more: The fbc value is built from the fbclid in the ad click URL, in a format like fb.1.<timestamp>.<fbclid>; the pixel creates it automatically, or your server can build it. At the time of writing, Meta shows an Event Match Quality score for each event in Events Manager. Field names and formats change, so copy them from the current Meta documentation, not from old blog posts.

rows: Click ID cookie built from fbclid
Browser ID cookie from the pixel

steps.say: The platform needs enough information to know which person an event belongs to. Look at the table. F B C is the click I D cookie built from the f b clid, not hashed. F B P is the browser I D cookie from the pixel, not hashed. Email and phone must be hashed with S H A two fifty six. External I D is your own user I D, and hashing is recommended. Client I P and user agent come from the visit, not hashed. More good fields mean better matching and better optimisation. Copy field names from Meta's current docs, not old blog posts.

steps.p: Hashing turns an email or phone into a fixed code the platform can compare without you sending the raw value. It only works if everyone prepares the data the same way.
steps.more: Example: ' Ada@Mail.com ' becomes 'ada@mail.com' before hashing. Phone '0803 123 4567' in Nigeria becomes '2348031234567'. Hashing protects data in transit and storage, but it is not anonymisation: a hashed email is still personal data under most data protection laws, so you still need a lawful basis and consent where required.
d: Phone with country code, digits only
Never hash fbc, fbp, IP or user agent
steps.say: Hashing turns an email or phone into a fixed code the platform can compare, without you sending the raw value. It only works if everyone prepares the data the same way. Go down the list: trim spaces, lowercase emails, phone with country code and digits only, then hash with S H A two fifty six. And never hash F B C, F B P, I P or user agent. One more thing: hashing is not anonymisation. A hashed email is still personal data under most data protection laws, so you still need a lawful basis, and consent where required.

steps.p: Every server event carries the same core pieces: what happened, when, a unique ID, who it was and where it happened. Miss one and the event is rejected or cannot be used for optimisation.
steps.say: Every server event carries the same core pieces. Read the line on screen: event name, plus event time, plus event I D, plus user data, plus action source. In plain words: what happened, when, a unique I D, who it was, and where it happened. Miss one, and the event is rejected, or it can't be used for optimisation.

steps.h: A server event for a deposit
steps.p: This is the shape of one server event for a first deposit. Your server fills it from the stored click row and the postback. Personal fields are hashed; fbc, IP and user agent are sent as they are. Field names follow Meta's docs at the time of writing; copy from the current docs.
steps.more: Which action_source fits a deposit that happened on the advertiser's site is set by Meta's rules, and the options have changed before. We are not certain which value Meta expects for every off-site case today; check the current Conversions API docs. The event_id here is the network's transaction ID, which the next lesson explains.

d.note: Simplified. Sent with your access token to your dataset's Conversions API endpoint. Never put the token in a page.

steps.say: The code on screen shows the shape of one server event for a first deposit. Your server fills it from the stored click row and the postback. Notice that personal fields are hashed, while F B C, I P and user agent are sent as they are. The value is forty, in U S dollars. Field names follow Meta's docs at the time of writing, so copy from the current docs. We're not certain which action source value Meta expects for every off-site case today, so check that too. And never put your access token in a page.

steps.p: Meta accepts server events with an event_time up to 7 days in the past at the time of writing. Deposits that arrive later cannot be sent. Send events as soon as the postback arrives; do not batch them weekly. Check the current docs.

d.text: Late events are rejected or ignored, and they teach the algorithm nothing.

steps.say: Timing matters. At the time of writing, Meta accepts server events with an event time up to seven days in the past. Deposits that arrive later can't be sent. So send each event as soon as the postback arrives, and don't batch them weekly. As the warning says, late events are rejected or ignored, and they teach the algorithm nothing. Check the current docs for the exact limit.

steps.h: Telegram join as a server event
steps.p: Meta cannot see a Telegram join, because it happens inside Telegram. A join tracking tool links each join back to the click that caused it and sends it to the platform as a server event.
steps.more: Tools such as Joinvoo do this by tying each join, via a per-click invite link or a join request, to the stored click, then sending a server event to Meta, TikTok or Snapchat. Whatever tool you use, check that it sends only real joins and that your privacy notice covers it.

b.title: With server events
items: Cost per join and per FTD measured

steps.say: Meta can't see a Telegram join, because it happens inside Telegram. Compare the two sides. Without server events, your ad optimises for link clicks, Meta finds people who click, many never join, and your cost per join is a guess. With server events, the join is sent as a conversion, Meta finds people who join, deposits can be sent too, and cost per join and per F T D are measured. A join tracking tool, such as Joinvoo, links each join to its click. Whatever tool you use, check it sends only real joins, and that your privacy notice covers it.

steps.p: Illustration of how many of 100 real registrations the ad platform receives with each setup. Browser events miss some people; server events fill most of the gap. Real numbers depend on your audience, devices and browsers.
steps.say: This chart is an illustration of how many of one hundred real registrations the platform receives with each setup. Look at the bars. Pixel only, an example of seventy. Server only, ninety two. Pixel plus server, deduplicated, ninety seven. Browser events miss some people, and server events fill most of the gap. Your real numbers will depend on your audience, devices and browsers.

steps.p: Sending people's data to an ad platform is processing personal data, whether it leaves from a browser or your server. Do it lawfully and openly, and make sure your privacy notice tells people what you do.
steps.more: Laws differ: GDPR in the EU and UK, Nigeria's NDPA 2023, Kenya's Data Protection Act 2019, South Africa's POPIA and Ghana's Data Protection Act 2012 all cover this kind of processing in different ways. Platforms also have their own terms on what data you may send, including bans on sensitive data. This is not legal advice; check with a professional for each geo.
d: Privacy notice names the ad platforms you share with
Ask for consent where the law requires it
Respect a refusal: no pixel, no server event
Keep a record of your setup
steps.say: Sending people's data to an ad platform is processing personal data, whether it leaves from a browser or your server. So go through this checklist. Your privacy notice names the ad platforms you share with. Ask for consent where the law requires it. Respect a refusal: no pixel, no server event. Send only the fields you need. And keep a record of your setup. Laws differ by country, including Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa and Ghana. This is not legal advice, so check with a professional for each geo.

steps.p: A join is the event most Telegram funnels need and the hardest to send yourself, because it happens inside Telegram. A join tracker ties each join request to the stored click and sends it as a server event. Check that it sends real joins only and that your privacy notice names it.

d.why: Sends each real Telegram join to the ad platform as a server event, tied to the click that caused it.

steps.say: A join is the event most Telegram funnels need, and the hardest to send yourself, because it happens inside Telegram. This card shows Joinvoo, a join tracker. It ties each join request to the stored click and sends each real Telegram join to the ad platform as a server event. As with any tool, check that it sends real joins only, and that your privacy notice names it.

steps.p: Example: you get 400 registrations a week. The pixel alone reports 260 to Meta. Adding server events with good matching raises it to 380. The algorithm now learns from 380 signals a week instead of 260, about 46% more data to optimise on.

d.text: 380 ÷ 260 ≈ 1.46, so about 46% more signals. Example figures.

steps.say: Here's a worked example. You get four hundred registrations a week. The pixel alone reports two hundred and sixty to Meta. Adding server events with good matching raises that to three hundred and eighty. Look at the maths on screen: three hundred and eighty divided by two hundred and sixty is about one point four six. So the algorithm learns from about forty six percent more signals each week. These are example figures.

steps.p: Meta's Events Manager has a test events tool. Send a test code with your server events and watch them arrive before you switch to live. Fix any error it shows. Names change; check the current Events Manager.

d.text: Never send fake or test conversions into a live dataset. They mislead the algorithm.

steps.say: Before you go live, test. Meta's Events Manager has a test events tool. You send a test code with your server events and watch them arrive before you switch to live, then fix any error it shows. And notice the warning: never send fake or test conversions into a live dataset, because they mislead the algorithm. Names change, so check the current Events Manager.

steps.p: Server events fail quietly. The platform accepts the call, but matching is poor or the event teaches the wrong thing. These five mistakes cause most of it, and each has a simple fix you can check in an afternoon.
d: Hashing fbc, IP or agent|send these as they are
Raw email or phone|trim, lowercase, SHA-256
Deposits batched weekly|send as each postback arrives
Test events in the live dataset|use the test code only
steps.say: Server events fail quietly. The platform accepts the call, but matching is poor, or the event teaches the wrong thing. Look at the five cards. Hashing F B C, I P or user agent: send these as they are. Raw email or phone: trim, lowercase, then S H A two fifty six. Deposits batched weekly: send them as each postback arrives. Test events in the live dataset: use the test code only. And ignoring consent: server-side is not exempt. Each of these is a simple fix you can check in an afternoon.

takeaways: Pixel events come from the browser; server events come from your server
Off-page events like joins and deposits can only be sent server-side
Good matching needs fbc, fbp, IP, user agent and hashed personal fields
Hashing is not anonymisation; you still need consent where required

quiz.q: Why can a pixel not report a first deposit at the broker?
options: The deposit happens off your page, where the pixel is not installed
The pixel only works on desktop
quiz.why: The pixel only sees events on pages where it runs. Deposits happen on the advertiser's site.

quiz.q: Which field must be hashed before sending?
quiz.why: Personal identifiers like email and phone are hashed with SHA-256. fbc, fbp, IP and user agent are sent as they are.

lessons.title: Deduplication and event_id
objectives: By the end you can explain why sending the same event twice is a problem
By the end you can generate and share an event_id between pixel and server
By the end you can find duplicate events in your reports
By the end you can decide which events need both browser and server sending

steps.p: When you send a registration from both the pixel and the server, the platform gets two messages about one real event. Unless it knows they are the same, it counts two registrations. Your cost per result looks half what it really is.

d.s: Counted once only if you say so

steps.say: Here's the problem. When you send a registration from both the pixel and the server, the platform gets two messages about one real event. Unless it knows they're the same, it counts two registrations. As the screen says: same event, sent twice, counted once only if you say so. And when results are doubled, your cost per result looks half of what it really is.

steps.p: Meta treats a browser event and a server event as duplicates when they share the same event name and the same event ID, and they arrive within its window. Then it keeps one.
steps.more: At the time of writing, Meta's docs describe deduplication when matching events arrive within 48 hours of each other. Meta also documents a fallback using fbp or external_id, but event_id is the reliable method. Other platforms, such as TikTok, use a similar event ID. Always check the current docs.
steps.say: So how does the platform know two messages are one event? Read the equation. Same event name, plus same event I D, equals counted once. Meta treats a browser event and a server event as duplicates when they share both, and arrive within its window. At the time of writing, Meta's docs describe that window as forty eight hours. There's a fallback, but the event I D is the reliable method. Other platforms, such as TikTok, use a similar I D. Always check the current docs.

steps.p: The trick is simple: create the ID once, at the moment the event happens, and give that same ID to both the pixel and the server. Any later step that makes a new ID breaks the match.
steps.say: The trick is simple. Follow the flow. The page creates the I D once, for example reg underscore eight f three k two a. The pixel sends with that event I D. The I D is saved with the lead. The server sends the same event I D. And the platform keeps one. Create the I D once, at the moment the event happens, and share it. Any later step that makes a new I D breaks the match.

steps.p: In code the idea is short. The page creates the ID once, gives it to the pixel and sends it to your server with the form. The server uses the same value as event_id. Field names are from Meta's docs at the time of writing; check the current docs.

d.note: The pixel option is eventID; the server field is event_id. Same value, same event name.

steps.say: In code, the idea is short. Look at the code on screen. In the browser, on form submit, the page creates the I D once. It gives it to the pixel, and sends it to your server with the form. Then the server uses the same value as its event I D. Notice the note at the bottom: the pixel option and the server field are spelled slightly differently, but they hold the same value, with the same event name. Field names are from Meta's docs at the time of writing, so check the current docs.

steps.p: Example: a registration form. On submit, the page creates reg_8f3k2a_1712345678. The pixel fires Lead with eventID reg_8f3k2a_1712345678. The form also posts that ID to your server, which sends a Lead server event with event_id reg_8f3k2a_1712345678.

d.text: Use something unique per event: the click ID plus a timestamp or an order number. Example IDs.

steps.say: Here's a worked example, a registration form. On submit, the page creates one I D: reg, then the click I D, then a timestamp. The pixel fires Lead with that I D. The form also posts the same I D to your server, which sends a Lead server event with the very same event I D. As the tip says, use something unique per event, like the click I D plus a timestamp, or an order number. These are example I Ds.

steps.p: The ID must be unique per real event and identical in both messages about that event. Most deduplication bugs come from breaking one of those two rules, or from event names that differ slightly.

a.title: Bad
items: New random ID in pixel and another in server
Missing in one of the two
Different event names: Lead vs lead_form

steps.say: There are two rules: the I D must be unique per real event, and identical in both messages about that event. Look at the bad column. Using the same I D for every event. A new random I D in the pixel and another in the server. The I D missing in one of the two. Or different event names, like Lead versus lead form. Now the good column: unique per real event, created once and shared, present in both sends, and exactly matching event names.

steps.p: Example: 100 real registrations sent by pixel and server without event_id. The platform reports nearly double, and your CPL looks far better than it is.

d.label: registrations reported for 100 real ones

steps.p: Not every event needs both senders. Send both only when the event can be seen in the browser and you want the server as a backup. Off-page events like deposits go server-only, with their own unique ID.
steps.say: Not every event needs both senders. Look down the table. Page view: browser yes, server optional. Registration on your form: both, with a shared event I D. Telegram join: server only. First deposit: server only. Repeat deposit: server only, with its own unique I D. The rule is, send both only when the event can be seen in the browser and you want the server as a backup. Off-page events go server only.

steps.p: A deposit sent only by your server can still be sent twice, for example if a network fires the same postback twice. Give each deposit a unique event_id, such as the network's transaction ID, so a retry does not count as a new deposit.

d.text: Use the network's transaction or conversion ID as the event_id for postback-driven events.

steps.say: Even server-only events can be sent twice. For example, a network might fire the same postback twice. So give each deposit a unique event I D, such as the network's transaction I D. Then a retry won't count as a new deposit. As the tip says, use the network's transaction or conversion I D as the event I D for postback-driven events.

lessons.title: Postbacks, event mapping and what to optimise for
objectives: By the end you can read a network postback and its macros
By the end you can map network statuses to ad platform events
By the end you can decide whether to optimise for lead, registration or FTD
By the end you can send conversion values and handle rejected conversions

steps.h: A postback is the network calling you
steps.p: A postback, or S2S call, is a request the network's server makes to your tracker's URL when something happens: a registration, a first deposit, a rejection. Macros in the URL are replaced with the details of that conversion.

d.b: Network to tracker, server to server

steps.say: A postback is the network calling you. It's also called an S two S call, server to server. When something happens, a registration, a first deposit or a rejection, the network's server makes a request to your tracker's U R L. Macros in that U R L are replaced with the details of the conversion. As the screen says, there's no browser involved.

steps.p: You give the network a URL with placeholders. The network fills them at conversion time. Macro names and brackets differ by network; copy them from your network's docs.
steps.say: Here's the anatomy of a postback U R L. Read the equation: your tracker U R L, plus a click I D slot filled from sub one, plus a status, plus a payout. You give the network a U R L with placeholders, and the network fills them in at conversion time. Macro names and brackets differ by network, so copy them from your network's docs.

steps.p: Every network names these macros differently, for example {sub1}, [sub_id] or {aff_sub}. The meanings are similar across networks. Copy the exact syntax from your network's documentation; a wrong bracket means an empty value.
steps.more: Some networks send one postback per event type; others send one URL with an event macro. Some only send approved conversions; others send pending, approved and rejected. Ask your manager exactly which events and statuses fire, how often, and whether a conversion can change status later. Write the answers down in your tracking notes.
steps.say: Every network names its macros differently, but the meanings are similar. Look down the table. Your click I D. The event or goal, like F T D, first time deposit. The status, like approved. The payout, like forty. The currency, like U S D. And the transaction I D. Copy the exact syntax from your network's documentation, because a wrong bracket means an empty value. Also ask your manager which events and statuses fire, and whether a conversion can change status later. Write the answers down.

steps.p: In most network dashboards the postback sits under tracking or postback settings, per offer or for all offers. Pick the event, paste the URL, then send a test. Names and layouts differ by network; ask your manager where yours is.

steps.h: Mapping network events to ad events
steps.p: You decide which ad platform event each network event becomes. Write this event map down, share it with your team and use it on every campaign, so reports mean the same thing everywhere.
steps.more: Standard event names, such as Lead, CompleteRegistration and Purchase, are understood by the platform's systems. Custom events give you clearer names but may need to be set up as custom conversions before you can optimise for them. Event names and options change; check the current Events Manager.
steps.say: You decide which ad platform event each network event becomes. That's your event map. Look down the table. A Telegram join becomes Lead or a custom Join, with no value. Registration becomes CompleteRegistration. An approved F T D becomes Purchase or a custom F T D, with the payout as its value. A qualified F T D becomes a custom Q F T D, with the payout. And rejected conversions? Do not send them. Write this map down, share it with your team, and use it on every campaign.

steps.p: You optimise for the deepest event that still gives the algorithm enough data to learn. Deeper events bring people more likely to pay, but there are fewer of them, so learning is slower and less stable.

a.title: Shallow (lead, join)
items: Good for new accounts and tests

steps.say: Which event should you optimise for? Compare the two sides. Shallow events, like a lead or a join, give many signals, learn fast and are cheaper, but can bring low-intent people. They're good for new accounts and tests. Deep events, like an F T D, give few signals, learn slowly and cost more, but bring people who pay. They're good once volume is steady. So you optimise for the deepest event that still gives the algorithm enough data to learn.

steps.p: Meta's guidance at the time of writing is that an ad set needs around 50 optimisation events in 7 days to leave the learning phase. If you cannot reach that on FTDs, optimise for a shallower event that strongly predicts deposits. Check the current guidance.

steps.p: Work out how many events each depth gives you per ad set per week. Then pick the deepest event that stays above about 50. Splitting budget across many ad sets lowers the count in each one.
steps.say: Here's how to choose the deepest usable event. Read the equation: weekly budget, divided by cost per event, divided by the number of ad sets, equals events per ad set. Work that out for each depth, then pick the deepest event that stays above about fifty. And notice: splitting budget across many ad sets lowers the count in each one.

steps.p: Sending the payout as the event value lets value-based bidding favour people who bring you more money. It only works when values are consistent, honest and in the same currency.
steps.more: With RevShare, your income per depositor grows over weeks, so the true value is unknown at the first deposit. Many operators send the first deposit with a fixed estimated value and track the real value in their tracker. Whatever you choose, apply it consistently, so the platform compares like with like.

steps.say: Sending the payout as the event value lets value-based bidding favour people who bring you more money. But it only works when values are consistent and honest. Go down the checklist. Send value and currency on deposit events. Use your payout, not the user's deposit, unless you choose otherwise. Use the same currency every time. Send no value on events that pay nothing. And do not inflate values. With RevShare, many operators send a fixed estimated value and track the real value in their tracker. Whatever you choose, apply it consistently.

steps.p: Networks may reject a conversion days or weeks later, for example for failed KYC, duplicate accounts or fraud. Plan in advance what happens to that conversion in your tracker and in your ad platform.

a.title: Ignore it
items: Platform keeps learning from bad events
Same bad source keeps getting budget

steps.say: Networks may reject a conversion days or weeks later, for example for failed K Y C, know your customer checks, duplicate accounts or fraud. Compare the two sides. If you ignore it, the platform keeps learning from bad events, your tracker profit is overstated, the same bad source keeps getting budget, and you get a surprise at payout time. If you handle it, your tracker marks it rejected, rejected events are never sent onward, you track rejection rate per source, and you cut sources with high rejections. Plan this in advance.

steps.h: Optimise on volume, decide on money
steps.p: Optimise on whatever event has enough volume, but make kill and scale calls on network-confirmed, approved conversions. The rule card in the Budget and kill rules module uses those: kill at 2 × target CPA with 0 conversions; scale +20% at 3+ conversions and CPA ≤ 0.8 × target. Starting rules.

d.text: Example: optimising on registrations, judged on approved FTDs. Target $30, $70 spent, 40 registrations, 0 FTDs: kill, after a plumbing check.

The rule card from the Budget and kill rules module says: kill at two times target C P A, cost per acquisition, with zero conversions. Scale by twenty percent at three or more conversions, with C P A at or below zero point eight times target. In the example, target thirty dollars, seventy spent, forty registrations, zero F T Ds: kill, after a plumbing check. These are starting rules.

steps.p: Postback mistakes are expensive because they hide in plain sight. Reports keep filling with numbers, but the numbers are empty, doubled or wrong. Check your setup against these five before every new offer.
d: Pending sent as deposits|rejections train the algorithm
No secret key|anyone can fake conversions
Event map not written down|each buyer maps differently
steps.say: Postback mistakes hide in plain sight. Reports keep filling with numbers, but the numbers are empty, doubled or wrong. Look at the five cards. Wrong macro brackets, so values arrive empty. Pending sent as deposits, so rejections train the algorithm. No transaction I D, so retries count twice. No secret key, so anyone can fake conversions. And an event map that isn't written down, so each buyer maps differently. Check your setup against these five before every new offer.

steps.h: Values must be what you earn
steps.p: Value-based bidding trusts the numbers you send. Inflating values, or sending a player's deposit amount as if it were your income, misleads the platform and your own reports. Send the payout you will actually be paid, in one currency, and fix any value you know is wrong.

d.text: Never send a value you were not paid, and never send rejected or test conversions to a live dataset.

lessons.title: Data quality, bots and fraud
objectives: By the end you can reconcile platform, tracker and network numbers
By the end you can spot bot and fraud patterns in your traffic
By the end you can filter bad events before they reach the ad platform
By the end you can run a weekly data quality check

steps.p: The ad platform learns from what you send it. Send fake joins, duplicate deposits or bot clicks and it will go and find more of the same. Clean data is the cheapest optimisation you will ever do.

d.s: Bad signal buys more bad traffic

steps.say: Garbage in, garbage out. The ad platform learns from what you send it. Send fake joins, duplicate deposits or bot clicks, and it will go and find more of the same. Look at the line on screen: the algorithm copies your signal, and bad signal buys more bad traffic. That's why clean data is the cheapest optimisation you'll ever do.

steps.p: The ad platform, your tracker and the network will never match exactly, because each counts in its own way. Your job is to know the normal gap between them and to notice quickly when that gap changes.
steps.more: Platforms report conversions inside their attribution window, by default often 7-day click and 1-day view on Meta at the time of writing, and may include modelled conversions. Networks count by their own approval rules and may report a deposit days later. The network is usually the number you get paid on, so treat it as the source of truth for money and the platform as the source for ad-level signals.
steps.say: You have three sources, and they'll never match exactly. Look at the table. The ad platform counts attributed results, and differs because of its attribution window and modelling. Your tracker counts clicks and matched conversions, and loses some to lost I Ds and blocked scripts. The network counts approved conversions, and differs because of holds, rejections and timing. The network is usually the number you get paid on, so treat it as the source of truth for money, and the platform as the source for ad-level signals.

steps.p: Example: the platform reports 100 FTDs and the network approves 82. If this gap is steady week to week, you can work with it. If it suddenly widens, investigate.

steps.p: Put the three counts for the same event side by side each week. Example: platform, tracker and network FTDs. The normal gap holds for two weeks, then the tracker count falls while the network holds steady. That points at your postback or click IDs, not at your ads.

steps.h: Signs of bot or fraud traffic
steps.p: No single sign proves fraud; a good creative can have a high CTR. Several signs together, in the same placement or source, are a strong warning that deserves a closer look before you spend more.
d: Odd timing|clicks at 3 a.m. in bursts
Same fingerprint|one IP or device, many joins
Data centre IPs|cloud servers, not phones
Zero engagement|join, no reads, leave fast
Impossible rates|CTR or CR far above normal
steps.say: Here are the signs of bot or fraud traffic. Look at the five cards. Odd timing, like clicks at three a.m. in bursts. The same fingerprint, one I P or device with many joins. Data centre I Ps, cloud servers instead of phones. Zero engagement: they join, read nothing, and leave fast. And impossible rates, a C T R, click-through rate, or conversion rate far above normal. No single sign proves fraud. But several together, in the same placement or source, are a strong warning.

steps.p: One placement in an example campaign. Huge click volume, almost nothing at the end. The drop between clicks and page loads is the first red flag.
steps.say: This funnel shows one suspicious placement in an example campaign. Five thousand clicks. Nine hundred page loads. Sixty Telegram joins. Four registrations. Zero F T Ds. Huge click volume, almost nothing at the end. Look at the first drop, from clicks to page loads. That's the first red flag.

steps.p: Filter at your server so suspect events never reach the ad platform. Keep the raw data, including what you filtered and why, so you can review your rules and share evidence with your network if needed.
steps.more: Telegram joins are a common weak point. Some joiners are bots or accounts that leave within minutes. A short hold, for example only sending a join event if the person is still a member after a set time, filters many of them. The cost is a slower signal, so find the balance for your funnel.
d: Drop events with no valid click ID
Drop repeat events with the same event_id
Hold joins that leave within minutes
Flag many conversions from one IP or device
Never send rejected or test conversions
steps.say: So filter at your server, so suspect events never reach the ad platform. Go down the checklist. Drop events with no valid click I D. Drop repeat events with the same event I D. Hold joins that leave within minutes. Flag many conversions from one I P or device. And never send rejected or test conversions. Keep the raw data, including what you filtered and why. A short hold on joins filters many bots, but it slows your signal, so find the balance for your funnel.

steps.p: Every event goes through one filter on your server before anything is sent onward. Everything is written to a raw log, including what was filtered and why. Only clean events reach the ad platform, and the log becomes your evidence when you talk to your network.
steps.say: This map shows where the filter sits. Follow it. Network postbacks and join events both flow into one server filter. From there, everything is written to a raw log, which you keep. Only clean events go on to the ad platform. And the raw log becomes your evidence when you talk to your network manager.

steps.p: When you suspect fraud, act on evidence, write down what you saw and keep it honest with your partners. Your network manager is more likely to help when you bring clear data instead of complaints.

a.title: Wrong response
items: Hide it and hope payouts clear

b.title: Right response
items: Request credits where the platform allows

steps.say: When you suspect fraud, act on evidence. Compare the two columns. The wrong response: hide it and hope payouts clear, blame the network without data, keep sending the events, and ignore placements. The right response: pause the source or placement, share evidence with your manager, stop sending those events, and request credits where the platform allows. Your network manager is more likely to help when you bring clear data instead of complaints.

steps.p: Example: Audience Network placement, $200 spend, 300 joins, 270 left within 1 hour, 0 FTDs. Feed placement, $200 spend, 180 joins, 160 still in after 7 days, 6 FTDs. Exclude the first placement and stop sending its joins as events.

d.text: Cost per retained join: $200 ÷ 30 ≈ $6.67 vs $200 ÷ 160 = $1.25. Example figures.

Look at the maths: about six dollars sixty seven per retained join, against one dollar twenty five. So exclude the first placement, and stop sending its joins as events. Example figures.

steps.p: Spend fifteen minutes every week on these checks and put the time in the calendar. Most tracking problems are cheap to fix when caught in the first week and expensive when found a month later.
d: Platform vs tracker vs network gap
Share of conversions with a click ID
Consent and privacy notice still accurate

Any duplicate event I Ds. Rejection rate per source. Retention of joins per placement. And whether your consent and privacy notice are still accurate. Most tracking problems are cheap to fix in the first week, and expensive when found a month later.

steps.p: Turn the warning signs into rules you apply every week, so a data problem stops decisions before it costs money. These are starting rules, not platform numbers; adapt them to your setup and vertical.
steps.more: Example: your normal platform-to-network gap is 18%. This week it is 31%, a move of 13 points, so you hold all kill and scale calls until you find the cause. A placement that keeps 20% of joins at 7 days when your normal is 60% is under half your normal, so you exclude it and stop sending its joins.

rows: No ad-level kill or scale calls

steps.say: Now turn those warning signs into starting rules. Look at the table. If the platform to network gap moves ten or more points from normal, investigate before decisions. If matched share is under ninety percent, no ad-level kill or scale calls. If seven-day join retention is under half your normal, exclude the placement and stop its events. If a source's rejection rate doubles, pause it and ask the network. For example, a normal gap of eighteen percent jumping to thirty one is a thirteen point move, so you hold all calls. Adapt these to your setup.

steps.p: When numbers look bad, do not buy joins, deposit yourself or send events for people who never converted to "teach" the algorithm. That is fraud against the network and false data to the platform, and it ends accounts and payouts. Find and cut the source of bad traffic instead.

d.text: Send only real events from real people. Report suspected fraud to your network with evidence.

steps.h: One setup, every decision after it
steps.p: Everything in this module comes together in one setup: a traffic source, an offer, a campaign link and a postback. Set it up carefully once and every later report is trustworthy. Set it up carelessly and every kill or scale call is a guess with real money behind it.

Set it up carelessly, and every kill or scale call is a guess with real money behind it. So in this lesson we'll go slowly, in order.

steps.p: This is the whole setup. The ad sends people through your tracker's campaign link to the lander and offer. The network calls your tracker back with a postback. Your tracker forwards clean events to the ad platform. Each arrow must carry the click ID.

exam.q: You see 60 FTDs in the network but only 25 in your tracker. Spend is $1,500. What is the first step?
options: Raise budget on the best ad
Find where the click ID is lost and fix it before judging campaigns
exam.why: 25 ÷ 60 is about 42% matched, far under the 90% gate, so ad-level decisions are guesses. Fix tracking first.

exam.q: Pixel and server both send Lead for form submissions. Meta shows 190 leads; your database has 100. Most likely cause?
options: Missing or mismatched event_id between pixel and server
exam.why: Nearly double counts point to failed deduplication.

exam.q: You want Meta to optimise for Telegram joins. What do you need?
options: A server event for each real join tied to the original click
exam.why: Meta cannot see joins; only a server event linked to the click can report them.

exam.q: Budget $2,000 a week, 4 ad sets, cost per FTD $30. Should you optimise for FTD?
options: No, about 17 per ad set is well below about 50
exam.why: 2,000 ÷ 30 ÷ 4 ≈ 17 per ad set, too few to learn well. Consolidate or use a shallower event.

exam.q: Your network sends pending, approved and rejected statuses. Which should become ad platform conversions?
options: Approved only, per your event map
exam.why: Send only events you count as real success; never send rejected ones.

exam.q: You launched with the postback "to add later". Day 3: your tracker shows 0 FTDs, the network shows 4. Target $30, one ad set has spent $70. What do you do?
options: Kill the ad set: $70 is past 2 × target with 0 FTDs
Set and test the postback, then judge the ad set on network-confirmed FTDs, not the tracker zero
Scale it because the network shows FTDs
exam.why: The tracker zero is a plumbing failure, not a result. Kill rules need network-confirmed data, so fix the postback first and judge on the network numbers.

exam.q: A visitor in a country that requires consent declines tracking. Your server could still send a CAPI event. Should it?
options: No, respect the refusal for pixel and server
exam.why: Consent covers the processing, not the technology. Hashing does not remove the need for consent.

exam.q: A placement brings 5,000 clicks, 900 page loads, 0 FTDs, mostly from data centre IPs. Best action?
options: Exclude the placement, stop sending its events and share evidence with your rep
exam.why: Strong bot signals: pause, filter and document.

exam.q: Target $30, payout $40. After 5 days an ad set has $96 spend and 5 network-confirmed FTDs, with a 92% matched share. What is the call?
options: Scale +20%: CPA $19.20 is 0.64 × target with 5 FTDs, then wait at least 48 hours
exam.why: Matching is above the 90% gate, so the numbers can be trusted. $96 ÷ 5 = $19.20, under the $24 scale line with 3+ FTDs.

exam.q: After you start filtering fast leavers, reported joins drop 30% while network FTDs stay flat. A teammate wants to undo it. What do you say?
options: Double the budget to recover joins
Keep it; you removed noise and deposits held, so cost per real result is clearer
exam.why: Reported joins fell because noise was removed. Real results held, and the algorithm now learns from better signal.
